title: The Omnipresence and Nature of the Spirit
english: Having appeared from a private opinion to be unproven, ungracious, and reckless, neither the Scripture saying that the Divine Spirit is a beginning, nor the Scripture euphemistically calling it 'Spirit of God' and 'from God' and 'divine' and 'holy', nor the Scripture not distinguishing between the first and the second regarding the nature of the divine hypostases, what dispute remains concerning them being in the unbegotten one Godhead and equality? [The opponent claims] that it fills the inhabited world and pervades all things, and that nothing created fills the inhabited world or pervades all things, and it is found in all; but rather it is the limit of the noetic powers and a defined quantity; for only these are proper to the Godhead.

But the greatness of the Holy Spirit is indissoluble, infinite, and everywhere, and through all, and in all always; filling the world and pervading according to the Godhead, yet uncontainable according to the power, and measuring indeed, but not being measured. 'For God does not give the Spirit according to measure,' as the Savior says in John (cf. John 3:8); and according to Wisdom, having [it]: 'For you love all existing things, and you loathe nothing of what you have made; for you would not have fashioned something if you hated it. How then would anything remain, if you had not willed it or if it had not been preserved by you? And spare all things, for all things are yours, O life-loving Lord, and your incorruptible Spirit is in all' (Wisdom 11:24-26). From this we appropriately name God the Father of all, not being our father by nature, as the Only-Begotten is.

And again: 'The Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world, and the one pervading all things has the voice of knowledge;' (cf. Ps 104:30) instead of [saying] that it has taken up the invisible and visible creation, the intelligible and sensible, and nothing of all things is without his eternal oversight; for this pervading of all things demonstrates it. And he says, it hearkens to the voice of all, as God always being in all and everywhere, and bringing every material disorder into the proper order, and being sparing toward those made by him.

And even while attending to it, since He Himself is providence and wisdom by nature, having been permeated through all things, just as the Father is. For who possesses such knowledge? Isaiah says thus: 'spirit of knowledge and reverence' (Isa 11:2), and David suggests: 'where shall I go from your face? and from your spirit where shall I flee?' (Ps 139:7). And the Lord, teaching that the divinity of the Holy Spirit is not circumscribed by place, but is simultaneously in heaven and upon the earth, always providing all sufficiency and providing to creation, said according to John: 'if you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that the spirit of truth may be with you, which the world cannot receive, it neither sees it nor knows it; but you know it, because it remains with you, and in you it shall be' (John 14:15-21).

In order that it might become known, how such testimonies manifest one single infinite nature present everywhere; they delivered the same things concerning another unmixed subsistence: Jeremiah, explaining from God and the Father, says: 'I fill the heaven and the earth, says the Lord' (Jer 23:24); David, singing about the Son in the 40th Psalm: 'and of his greatness there is no end' (Ps 72:5); and Paul, preaching about the same: 'he is the one who descended and the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things' (Eph 4:10).

6.3 That creation, though incorruptible, is not absolutely incorrupt; rather it receives corruption, the nourishment which we say, and change, as the prophecy says: 'the one doing all things and reshaping them.' The wise men from without, having heard this, say: 'dissolving things into themselves, and from them again growing.' For the incorporeal rational creation has corruption according to choice, since God alone has given it a permanent nature, and having established it unto the age, and unto the age of ages; but it, changing by its own choice, falls into a worse state, and to it...
